brique._comment: Engine-native Execution family capacity. kind/wrapper/rel_ctx/lang do not apply here.

objective.name: wrapper.start
objective.description: Start a named wrapper in the current context. Builds if necessary, then starts the process and waits for readiness.

#root.role: Resolve the named wrapper configuration, build if required, start the process, wait for readiness, and emit a response.

name._comment: Required. Name of the wrapper to start, as declared in engine_config.execution.wrappers.

payload._comment: Empty payload on success. The wrapper is running and ready when the response is received.

effects.wrapper_runtime: The wrapper process is started. Build artifacts may be produced if the wrapper requires compilation.

transformation_contract.morphing: A start request becomes a running, ready wrapper process.
invariants: params.name must refer to a wrapper declared in the addressed context's OWN execution config — resolution is strictly local per context, with no inheritance from a parent context's execution.wrappers, however architecturally close. A wrapper declared in a parent is never reachable by wrapper.start (or by any capacity) addressed at a child context; the wrapper must be declared, and wrapper.start invoked, against the exact context that owns it. Fails with reason=wrapper_not_configured otherwise.
The handler runs asynchronously — it does not block the execution inbox.

Readiness requires the wrapper process to connect back to the engine over its own websocket route and send wrapper_ready. This requires THREE separate context.json declarations to agree: engine_config.execution.wrappers[].wrapper_name, engine_config.communication.wrapper_boundary (same name, enables routing), and an engine_config.communication.interfaces[] entry with type='wrapper' and the same name (opens the actual channel the process connects through). The engine does not cross-check these three at startup or during wrapper.start — if the interfaces[] entry is missing while the other two are present, the process starts but can never connect, and wrapper.start observes no different failure mode than any other unready process: it times out.
success: Emits an OK response with empty payload when the wrapper is ready.
failure: Emits an error response when the wrapper name is missing or not configured.
Emits an error response when the build or start process fails.

Times out with a generic 'wrapper readiness timeout' error (no distinguishing detail) when the process started but never signaled readiness — including the case where its required interfaces[] entry (type='wrapper', matching name) is missing from context.json. If wrapper.start times out, verify all three declarations noted above are present before assuming a build or process-level failure.
